edits_applied.before: Take the whole affair apart and the lord is never choosing between good and bad; what stood before him were courses of action that were all dirty: appeal to the king (a dead end), go die alone (useless), forge an order and seize the army (proposed by Hou Ying; a wound to his own state). The author's inference is that Hou Ying's line about throwing meat to a starving tiger is what forced him to trade courage for a plan. The author's counterfactual: had he not turned back, he would most likely have died with his hundred-odd chariots of retainers in front of the Qin lines, Handan might never have been relieved, and there would have been no army marching against Qin afterward.

edits_applied.before: The plan covered only the first half; the second half was the bad case. Hou Ying warned that "a general in the field is not bound by every order from his sovereign": even with the tallies matching, if Jin Bi withheld the army and sent to the king instead, the whole enterprise would be in danger. So take the butcher Zhu Hai along: "If Jin Bi obeys, excellent; if not, you may have him strike." Lord Xinling wept on hearing it: "Jin Bi is a battle-seasoned old general; I fear he will not obey, and then he must be killed. That is why I weep. Do you imagine I fear death?" What he cried for was the killing of his own country's veteran commander, not the risk to himself. Zhu Hai said he was a butcher who slapped the knife in the marketplace; he had never returned the lord's visits because "petty courtesies were of no use" — but "now that the lord is in a tight spot, this is the hour to spend my life." Hou Ying said he was too old to go, and asked to count the days of the journey, so that "on the day you reach Jin Bi's camp I shall face north and cut my own throat, to see you off."

edits_applied.before: The third is the accounting afterward. The retainer's words — "a service to Zhao, but not the act of a loyal minister to Wei" — keep both columns straight: the credit belongs to Zhao, the debt to Wei. His response was not to argue but to blame himself on the spot, then send the army home and stay in Zhao, acknowledging the debt through departure. One reading: his refusal to claim credit chimes with the self-blame that followed — the welcome at the border came first, and the retainer's rebuke, the self-reproach, and staying in Zhao came after.
